advances: The actual original cubic-depth bound on the complete log-affine height-tree support extends to every coordinate-dependent spatial field in the critical cube, and more generally to fields with bounded total absolute variation along the blocks of any rooted path. The new step is a weighted complete-continuation census obtained by adaptively revealing disjoint blocks under a nonidentical Bernoulli product law. The same full-normalizer estimate also gives an explicit sufficient product-surplus condition for arbitrary spatial fields. These statements concern this exact support family, rather than arbitrary log-concave lattice laws.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. Accepted fact 032423921efad6c8 supplies the exact tree, successor injection, and inverse reconstruction. Accepted fact 604889294a17d7df supplies the exact height support and \(\eta^Q>3/4\). The actual neighbor-and-endpoint halfspace mechanism of accepted fact d9c4b095a13caaba is used with its points and scalar costs displayed in the proof. The nonidentical-field adaptive census, full tilted normalizer, weight comparison, moment substitution, and product-surplus inequality are proved here.
proof:
Write \(\eta=1-2^{-m}\binom m{m/2}\). Since \(b_8=4\), one has \(Q\ge4\) and \(m\ge1250\). Accepted fact 032423921efad6c8 gives \(|D_m|=|\operatorname{im}F_m|=2^m\eta\), the successor injection, the exact forward construction, and the inverse reconstruction used below. Accepted fact 604889294a17d7df supplies the exact height support for \(\rho_t=2^{-t}\) and \(\eta^Q>3/4\). There is no change of parameters or normalization in consuming these facts.

We first establish a census that allows different fields at different tree coordinates. For an arbitrary vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(L_\lambda=\lVert\lambda\rVert_\infty\), and let \(Z_\lambda=\prod_u(1+e^{\lambda_u})\). Give Boolean vectors the product law \(\mu_\lambda(b)=e^{\lambda\cdot b}/Z_\lambda\); its coordinate \(u\) has success probability \(e^{\lambda_u}/(1+e^{\lambda_u})\).

At any fixed child block, every Boolean pattern \(c\) has probability at least \(2^{-m}e^{-mL_\lambda}\). Indeed, the ratio of each coordinate's probability to its fair-bit probability is \(2e^{\lambda_uc_u}/(1+e^{\lambda_u})\ge e^{-|\lambda_u|}\). Thus each of the two sets \(D_m\) and \(\operatorname{im}F_m\) has block probability at least \(\eta e^{-mL_\lambda}\), uniformly over the block's location.

Fix \(s\in\lbrace0,\ldots,Q\rbrace\). On a Boolean vector \(b\), perform the following mixed exploration. For the first \(s\) steps require the current child block to be in \(D_m\), and choose the next child by its forward successor index. For the remaining \(Q-s\) steps require the current child block to be in \(\operatorname{im}F_m\), and choose the next child by \(i_m(F_m^{-1}(b[v]))\). Stop at the first failure, and let \(E_s\) be the event that all \(Q\) steps succeed.

This adaptive exploration reveals only fresh blocks. After \(r-1\) successful steps, their blocks consist of coordinates at respective depths \(1,\ldots,r-1\), while the next block has depth \(r\). The next node is determined by the already revealed patterns. More precisely, a fixed successful transcript specifies those patterns at their thereby determined locations and imposes no constraint on any unrevealed coordinate: every assignment to the other coordinates produces that same transcript. It is consequently a cylinder event for exactly the revealed blocks. Under the product law, conditional on any such transcript, the next block retains its original product marginal, even though this marginal depends on the selected node. The preceding uniform block estimate therefore bounds each conditional success probability below by \(\eta e^{-mL_\lambda}\). Summing over transcripts at each step and iterating proves \(\mu_\lambda(E_s)\ge\eta^Qe^{-mQL_\lambda}\). This argument integrates over all unused blocks; it makes no identical-distribution assumption.

Let \(\mathcal C_s\) consist of the level-\(s\) points whose canonical inverse reconstruction continues through level \(Q\), as in accepted fact d9c4b095a13caaba. There is a bijection between \(E_s\) and \(\mathcal C_s\): on \(E_s\), change the selected zero to two in each of the first \(s\) explored blocks and leave every other coordinate unchanged. The resulting point \(j=z_s(b)\) is in the original support. The remaining mixed-exploration tests are precisely its inverse reconstruction, since its blocks beyond the forward prefix are still Boolean and unchanged. Conversely, from a complete \(j\), replacing its \(s\) twos by zeros recovers its unique Boolean source \(b\); its forward prefix and injective inverse suffix recover exactly the mixed exploration. Thus this operation is onto and one-to-one. Its weight multiplier is \(e^{2\sum_{r=1}^{s}\lambda_{u_r}}\ge e^{-2QL_\lambda}\). It follows that
$$
\sum_{j\in\mathcal C_s}e^{\lambda\cdot j}
\ge e^{-2QL_\lambda}Z_\lambda\mu_\lambda(E_s)
\ge\eta^Qe^{-(m+2)QL_\lambda}Z_\lambda
\qquad(0\le s\le Q).
$$

There is a second useful census in terms of \(\Pi(\lambda)\). A complete successful transcript fixes exactly the \(Q\) disjoint visited blocks. Its probability under \(\mu_\lambda\) is the product of their pattern probabilities; all unused coordinates integrate to one. Dividing by its probability under fair bits gives a ratio at least \(e^{-\sum_{r=0}^{Q-1}\sum_i|\lambda_{v_ri}|}\ge e^{-\Pi(\lambda)}\). Different complete successful transcripts define disjoint cylinders: if two differ, their first differing revealed pattern occurs at the same node, determined by their common earlier patterns. Under fair bits, each next required set has conditional probability \(\eta\), so the total probability of these successful cylinders is \(\eta^Q\). Summing the transcript comparison proves \(\mu_\lambda(E_s)\ge e^{-\Pi(\lambda)}\eta^Q\). The selected prefix coordinates are a subset of the coordinates in these visited blocks, and their absolute field sum is at most \(\Pi(\lambda)\). The bijection's spike multiplier is therefore at least \(e^{-2\Pi(\lambda)}\), giving the additional bound
$$
\sum_{j\in\mathcal C_s}e^{\lambda\cdot j}
\ge\eta^Qe^{-3\Pi(\lambda)}Z_\lambda
\qquad(0\le s\le Q).
$$

For every level \(s\), the unique-source map \(b\mapsto z_s(b)\), restricted to \(h(b)\ge s\), has spatial multiplier at most \(e^{2QB}\), and also at most \(e^{2\Pi(\gamma)}\). For the latter assertion, extend its rooted prefix to any path of depth \(Q\); the sum of the selected coordinates' absolute fields is at most that path's block sum. Thus that level's spatial weight is at most \(e^{2\min\lbrace QB,\Pi(\gamma)\rbrace}Z_\gamma\). Summing every height in every original column gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
W&\le e^{2\min\lbrace QB,\Pi(\gamma)\rbrace}Z_\gamma R_k,\\
R_k&\le2+2\sum_{\ell=8}^{k}b_\ell2^{-\ell}
\le2+\frac{H_k-H_7}{4}
\le\frac{9+\log k}{4},
\end{aligned}
$$
where \(H_j=\sum_{r=1}^{j}1/r\). The last inequality uses \(H_k\le1+\log k\). Also \((1+x)^4\le8(1+x^4)\) for \(x>0\), by convexity of the fourth power, so \(Z_{4\gamma}/Z_\gamma^4\ge8^{-n}\).

We next use the actual-halfspace selection mechanism of accepted fact d9c4b095a13caaba; the following details specify its selected original points and their spatial displacements. Suppose \(k\ge2^{16}\), and put \(u=\lfloor\sqrt{k}\rfloor\), \(v=2u\). Then \(u\ge256\), \(v\le k\), and \(\log k\ge16\log2>32/3>9\). Define
$$
\mathcal G=\left\lbrace(j,a_s+1):j\in\mathcal C_s,\quad8\le a_s\le u\right\rbrace,
\qquad
U=\sum_{\ell=8}^{u}b_\ell2^{-\ell},\quad
T=\sum_{\ell=v}^{k}b_\ell2^{-\ell}.
$$
All these sampled heights belong to the original columns. The floor bounds and harmonic integral estimates give
$$
\begin{aligned}
U&\ge\frac{H_u-H_7}{8}-\frac1{128}
\ge\frac{\log k}{16}-\frac{H_7}{8}-\frac1{128}
\ge\frac{\log k}{32},\\
T&\ge\frac{H_k-H_{v-1}}8-2^{1-v}
\ge\frac18\log\frac{k+1}{v}-2^{1-v}
\ge\frac{\log k}{16}-\frac{\log2}{8}-2^{1-v}
\ge\frac{\log k}{32}.
\end{aligned}
$$
For the last inequalities, \(H_7=363/140<13/5\) gives \(H_7/8+1/128<1/3<(\log k)/32\); also \(\log2<1\), \(v\ge512\), and \((\log k)/32>1/3\). Here \(H_u\ge\log(u+1)>(\log k)/2\) and \(v\le2\sqrt{k}\). The estimate \(\log2>2/3\) follows by integrating the tangent line to \(1/x\) at \(3/2\) over \([1,2]\).

Fix \(\mathbf I=(j,h)\in\mathcal G\), with \(s=\operatorname{level}(j)\) and \(h=a_s+1\). Its complete inverse continuation gives distinct coordinates \(u_{s+1},\ldots,u_Q\), with \(j_{u_r}=1\). Set \(V_r=\sum_{\ell=s+1}^{r}e_{u_\ell}\). By the reconstruction in 032423921efad6c8, the original base points \(j-V_r\) and \(j+V_r\) have respective levels \(s\) and \(r\). The base point \(j-e_{u_r}\) also has level \(s\) and belongs to \(A_{m,Q}\): replacing this suffix coordinate by zero leaves the first \(s\) forward blocks intact. Thus \((j-e_{u_r},a_s)\) and \((j\pm V_r,a_r)\) are actual original indices whenever used below.

Take a proper closed halfspace through \(\mathbf I\), written
$$
H=\left\lbrace(z,t):c^{\mathsf T}(z-j)+\theta(t-h)\ge0\right\rbrace,
\qquad(c,\theta)\ne(0,0).
$$
If \(\theta\ge0\), for every \(r\) with \(a_r\ge v>h\), at least one of \((j-V_r,a_r)\) and \((j+V_r,a_r)\) lies in \(H\). Their halfspace values are \(\pm c^{\mathsf T}V_r+\theta(a_r-h)\). The chosen indices are distinct across \(r\): lower endpoints have different \(V_r\), upper endpoints have different levels, and their levels distinguish these two families. Their total untilted weight \(2^{-t}\) is at least \(T\).

If \(\theta<0\), put \(\beta=-\theta>0\). Call \(r>s\) bad when \(c_{u_r}\le\beta\), and let \(L\) be the number of bad indices. Each distinct bad neighbor \((j-e_{u_r},a_s)\) lies in \(H\), because its halfspace value is \(\beta-c_{u_r}\ge0\). If \(L\ge2^{a_s}(\log k)/128\), these neighbors have total untilted weight at least \((\log k)/128\).

Otherwise let \(S_r=\beta^{-1}c^{\mathsf T}V_r\). In any maximal run of nonbad indices, successive increments exceed one, so at most \(2k+1\) values lie in \([-k,k]\). There are at most \(L+1\) runs and at most \(L\) bad indices. Since \(L<2^{a_s}(\log k)/128\) and \(a_s\le u\), one has \(L+1\le2^u\log k\), and consequently
$$
\bigl|\lbrace r:s<r\le Q,\ |S_r|\le k\rbrace\bigr|
\le(2k+2)(L+1)\le4k\,2^u\log k.
$$
For each remaining \(r\) with \(a_r\ge v\), one of the two original endpoints lies in \(H\), since its halfspace value is \(\beta(|S_r|-(a_r-h))>0\). The discarded indices lose at most \(4k2^u(\log k)2^{-v}\) from \(T\). Thus the selected distinct endpoints have untilted weight at least
$$
T-4k2^{-u}\log k\ge\frac{\log k}{32}-\frac{\log k}{64}
=\frac{\log k}{64}.
$$
Here \(2^u\ge256k\): \(k<(u+1)^2\), the ratio \(2^u/(u+1)^2\) increases for integers \(u\ge2\), and \(2^{256}>256\cdot257^2\).

Every containing proper halfspace contains a parallel one through \(\mathbf I\). The preceding cases therefore select, inside every containing halfspace, actual original indices of total untilted weight at least \((\log k)/128\). Each selected spatial point differs from \(j\) in at most \(Q\) coordinates, each by one in absolute value. Its tilted spatial weight is accordingly at least \(e^{\gamma\cdot j-QB}\). If \(\nu=\sum_{\mathbf J\in\widehat A}w_{\mathbf J}\delta_{\mathbf J}\) and \(h_\nu(\mathbf I)=W\tau_p(\mathbf I)\), the selected weights give
$$
h_\nu(\mathbf I)\ge e^{\gamma\cdot j-QB}\frac{\log k}{128}
\qquad(\mathbf I=(j,a_s+1)\in\mathcal G).
$$
This is a bound for every original containing halfspace. Only its selected points were compared; no bounded density ratio between the full measures was used.

The same selected-point comparison also gives \(h_\nu(\mathbf I)\ge e^{\gamma\cdot j-\Pi(\gamma)}(\log k)/128\). Indeed, the coordinates changed by any selected neighbor or endpoint lie in the child blocks of the complete rooted path through \(j\). Their absolute field sum is at most \(\Pi(\gamma)\).

We now sum under the original sampling law, including the fourth power of its full normalizer. Apply the proved complete-point census to \(\lambda=4\gamma\), whose norm is \(4B\). It gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
M_3(p)
&=W^{-4}\sum_{\mathbf I\in\widehat A}w_{\mathbf I}h_\nu(\mathbf I)^3\\
&\ge\frac{e^{-3QB}(\log k)^3}{128^3W^4}
 \sum_{\substack{s:8\le a_s\le u}}2^{-(a_s+1)}
 \sum_{j\in\mathcal C_s}e^{4\gamma\cdot j}\\
&\ge\frac{\eta^Q e^{-(4m+11)QB}Z_{4\gamma}\,U(\log k)^3}
 {2\cdot128^3W^4}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Because \(\log k>9\), the proved normalizer estimate is \(W\le e^{2QB}Z_\gamma(\log k)/2\). Substituting it together with \(U\ge(\log k)/32\) and \(\eta^Q>3/4\) yields
$$
M_3(p)\ge3\cdot2^{-25}e^{-(4m+19)QB}
 \frac{Z_{4\gamma}}{Z_\gamma^4}.
$$
If \(B\le1/(mQ)\), then \((4m+19)QB\le4+19/m<5\). The coordinatewise fourth-power inequality and \(N=n+1\) therefore give
$$
M_3(p)\ge3\cdot2^{-25}e^{-5}8^{-n}
=3\cdot2^{-22}e^{-5}8^{-N}>2^{-30}8^{-N}.
$$
For the final strict inequality, \(e<3\) implies \(e^5<243<256\). This proves the critical-cube claim for \(k\ge2^{16}\), with no restriction on the signs or equality pattern of the coordinates of \(\gamma\).

For the path-variation class, repeat that same moment substitution using the second depth bound, the second census at \(4\gamma\), and \(W\le e^{2\Pi(\gamma)}Z_\gamma(\log k)/2\). Since \(\Pi(4\gamma)=4\Pi(\gamma)\), the census costs \(12\Pi(\gamma)\), the cubed depth costs \(3\Pi(\gamma)\), and the fourth normalizer costs \(8\Pi(\gamma)\). The same numerical factors consequently give
$$
M_3(p)\ge3\cdot2^{-25}e^{-23\Pi(\gamma)}
 \frac{Z_{4\gamma}}{Z_\gamma^4}
\ge3\cdot2^{-22}e^{-23}8^{-N}>2^{-60}8^{-N}
\quad(\Pi(\gamma)\le1).
$$
For the last inequality, \(e^{23}<3^{23}<2^{37}\), since \(3^5<2^8\) and \(3^3<2^5\). This proves the more general claim in the large-height range.

For every \(k\ge8\) and every field \(\gamma\), the Boolean base points at height zero are original atoms. Every halfspace containing an atom includes its own mass, so \(\tau_p(\mathbf I)\ge p_{\mathbf I}\). The sum of fourth powers of the unnormalized weights of just these Boolean atoms is exactly \(Z_{4\gamma}\). Thus the already proved full-normalizer estimate gives the universal atom inequality
$$
\begin{aligned}
M_3(p)&\ge\frac{Z_{4\gamma}}{W^4}
\ge e^{-8\min\lbrace QB,\Pi(\gamma)\rbrace}R_k^{-4}\frac{Z_{4\gamma}}{Z_\gamma^4}\\
&=8^{-n}e^{-8\min\lbrace QB,\Pi(\gamma)\rbrace}R_k^{-4}\mathcal P(\gamma).
\end{aligned}
$$
Every factor of \(\mathcal P(\gamma)\) is at least one by \((1+x)^4\le8(1+x^4)\). This proves the arbitrary-field assertion and its stated sufficient surplus conditions, under exactly the original measure.

Finally, if \(8\le k<2^{16}\) and \(B\le1/(mQ)\), then \(\log k<16\) and \(R_k<8\). The same atom inequality with \(\mathcal P(\gamma)\ge1\) gives
$$
M_3(p)\ge e^{-8/m}8^{-4}8^{-n}
=e^{-8/m}2^{-9}8^{-N}>2^{-10}8^{-N}\ge2^{-30}8^{-N}.
$$
Indeed \(8/m\le8/1250<2/3<\log2\). Both height ranges preserve every original spatial point, every original column height, the full normalizer, and every actual ambient halfspace. All the estimates use the chosen chain partition only through the stated successor and cardinality properties, so they hold for every allowed partition.

In the same small-height range, \(\Pi(\gamma)\le1\) instead gives \(M_3(p)\ge e^{-8}2^{-9}8^{-N}>2^{-22}8^{-N}\ge2^{-60}8^{-N}\). Here \(e^8<3^8<2^{13}\). This completes all claims, including both weak boundary inequalities.
statement:
Fix an integer \(k\ge8\). Define \(b_\ell=0\) for \(1\le\ell<8\), and define \(b_\ell=\lfloor2^\ell/(8\ell)\rfloor\) for \(8\le\ell\le k\). Put \(Q_0=0\), \(Q_\ell=\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}b_r\), \(Q=Q_k\), \(m=2(Q+1)^4\), \(n=\sum_{r=1}^{Q}m^r\), and \(N=n+1\). Let \(a_0=0\), and let \(a_s=\ell\) whenever \(Q_{\ell-1}<s\le Q_\ell\). Thus \(k\) is the height parameter, \(m\) is the branching number, \(Q\) is tree depth, \(n\) counts spatial coordinates, and \(N\) counts all integer coordinates.

Choose any partition of \(\lbrace0,1\rbrace^m\) into symmetric saturated chains, as in accepted fact 032423921efad6c8. Let \(D_m\) consist of the nonterminal vertices, and let \(F_m:D_m\longrightarrow\lbrace0,1\rbrace^m\) be its injective chain successor, written \(F_m(c)=c+e_{i_m(c)}\), where \(c_{i_m(c)}=0\). Spatial coordinates are indexed by \(\mathcal T_{m,Q}=\bigcup_{r=1}^{Q}\lbrace1,\ldots,m\rbrace^r\). For a node \(v\) of depth less than \(Q\), including the empty root, its child block is \(x[v]=(x_{v1},\ldots,x_{vm})\).

For a Boolean vector \(b\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^{\mathcal T_{m,Q}}\), the canonical forward path starts at the root and, at a visited node \(v\), proceeds to \(vi_m(b[v])\) if \(b[v]\in D_m\). It stops on failure or at depth \(Q\), with length \(h(b)\) and selected coordinates \(u_1,\ldots,u_{h(b)}\). Retain the exact support from accepted facts 032423921efad6c8 and 604889294a17d7df:
$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{m,Q}&=\left\lbrace z_s(b)=b+2\sum_{r=1}^{s}e_{u_r}:
 b\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^{\mathcal T_{m,Q}},\quad0\le s\le h(b)\right\rbrace,\\
\widehat A&=\left\lbrace(z,t):z\in A_{m,Q},\quad
 a_{\operatorname{level}(z)}\le t\le k,\quad t\in\mathbb Z\right\rbrace.
\end{aligned}
$$
The level of \(z_s(b)\) is \(s\), equivalently the number of its coordinates equal to two.

For any vector \(\gamma=(\gamma_u)_{u\in\mathcal T_{m,Q}}\in\mathbb R^n\), put \(B=\lVert\gamma\rVert_\infty\). Define its path variation by
$$
\Pi(\gamma)=\max_{v_0,\ldots,v_Q}
 \sum_{r=0}^{Q-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}|\gamma_{v_ri}|,
$$
where the maximum ranges over every rooted path with \(v_0=\varnothing\) and \(v_{r+1}\) a child of \(v_r\). Define all original weights, their full normalizer, and the normalized law by
$$
w_{(z,t)}=\exp(\gamma\mathbin{\cdot}z)2^{-t}
\quad((z,t)\in\widehat A),\qquad
W=\sum_{\mathbf I\in\widehat A}w_{\mathbf I},\qquad
p_{\mathbf I}=w_{\mathbf I}/W.
$$
All other integer weights are zero. Use the actual ambient halfspace depth
$$
\tau_p(\mathbf I)=\inf\left\lbrace
 \sum_{\mathbf J\in H\cap\widehat A}p_{\mathbf J}:
 H\subseteq\mathbb R^N\text{ is a closed halfspace containing }\mathbf I
\right\rbrace,
\qquad
M_3(p)=\sum_{\mathbf I\in\widehat A}p_{\mathbf I}\tau_p(\mathbf I)^3.
$$
Then every such partition and every coordinate field with \(B\le1/(mQ)\), including the boundary, satisfy \(M_3(p)\ge2^{-30}8^{-N}\). More generally, every field with \(\Pi(\gamma)\le1\) satisfies \(M_3(p)\ge2^{-60}8^{-N}\). The critical cube is contained in this latter class because \(\Pi(\gamma)\le mQB\).

For arbitrary \(\gamma\), without the critical-cube restriction, define
$$
R_k=\sum_{s=0}^{Q}\sum_{t=a_s}^{k}2^{-t},\qquad
\mathcal P(\gamma)=\prod_{u\in\mathcal T_{m,Q}}
 \frac{8(1+e^{4\gamma_u})}{(1+e^{\gamma_u})^4}.
$$
One always has
$$
M_3(p)\ge8^{-n}e^{-8\min\lbrace QB,\Pi(\gamma)\rbrace}R_k^{-4}\mathcal P(\gamma),
\qquad R_k\le\frac{9+\log k}{4},\qquad\mathcal P(\gamma)\ge1.
$$
In particular, either explicit sufficient condition \(\log\mathcal P(\gamma)\ge8QB+4\log R_k\) or \(\log\mathcal P(\gamma)\ge8\Pi(\gamma)+4\log R_k\) implies \(M_3(p)\ge8^{-n}\ge8^{-N}\). The stronger, fully elementary conditions obtained by replacing \(R_k\) by \((9+\log k)/4\) also suffice. No assertion is made that every field outside the proved classes satisfies a surplus condition. All logarithms are natural.
